summary: A null pointer is a pointer that deliberately points at no object. It is the standard 'nothing here' value and the guard that separates safe code from crashes.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body: The C standard defines a null pointer constant as an integer constant expression with value 0, or such an expression cast to `void *`. The macro `NULL` (from `<stddef.h>`, `<stdio.h>`, `<stdlib.h>`) expands to it. Comparing any pointer to NULL tells you whether it refers to an object.
sections.code:
int *p = NULL;
if (p == NULL) { /* nothing to use */ }

sections.heading: Where NULL is used
bullets: Initializing pointers before they have a target.
Signalling failure: `malloc`, `fopen`, and `strstr` return NULL on failure or no match.
Marking the end of linked lists, trees, and argument vectors (`argv[argc]` is NULL).
Optional parameters: pass NULL to mean 'not provided'.

sections.heading: Checking allocation results
What happens on dereference
sections.body: Dereferencing NULL is undefined behavior. On common desktop systems page zero is unmapped, so you get a segmentation fault, but the standard does not promise that, and optimizers may assume it never happens.

sections.heading: NULL vs void* vs uninitialized
bullets: NULL is a value meaning 'no object'; it can be assigned to any pointer type.
`void *` is a type: a generic pointer that can hold any object address.
An uninitialized pointer holds garbage (a wild pointer) and is dangerous because you cannot test it.

subtopics.title: Set pointers to NULL after free
subtopics.summary: A cheap defence against double-free and use-after-free.

sections.body: `free(NULL)` is defined to do nothing, so nulling a pointer after freeing makes an accidental second free harmless and makes later NULL checks meaningful.

subtopics.title: Null is not necessarily all-zero bits

sections.body: The source-level constant 0 converts to a null pointer, but the machine representation of a null pointer may not be all zero bits on exotic platforms. Always compare with NULL, never `memcmp` against zeros.
Public functions should check pointer parameters and return an error code; internal helpers may document 'must not be NULL' and use `assert`. Static analyzers can then flag callers that pass NULL.
C++11 added `nullptr` and C23 adopted it, giving null a dedicated type so it cannot be confused with the integer 0 in overload or variadic contexts.

takeaways: NULL means 'points at nothing'; always check before dereferencing.
Functions signal failure by returning NULL; test the result.
NULL is a value; void* is a type; uninitialized pointers are neither.
